questions.text:
The formation of methane from its elements is represented by:

C(s) + 2H2(g) -> CH4(g)

Calculate DrH for this reaction using Hess's law, given the following standard enthalpies of combustion:

C(s) + O2(g) -> CO2(g)   DrH = -394 kJ mol-1
H2(g) + 1/2 O2(g) -> H2O(l)   DrH = -286 kJ mol-1
CH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2H2O(l)   DrH = -890 kJ mol-1

For Achievement:

For Merit:

questions.text:
Justify, in terms of the entropy changes of the system and the surroundings, why the combustion of methane is spontaneous.

CH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2H2O(l)   DrH = -890 kJ mol-1
questions.expectedAnswer: The combustion is highly exothermic (DrH = -890 kJ mol-1), so a large amount of heat is released to the surroundings. This increases the entropy of the surroundings (DS_surr = -DrH / T is positive). The system changes from 3 mol of gas (1 CH4 + 2 O2) to 1 mol of gas (CO2) plus 2 mol of liquid water, so the system entropy decreases (DS_sys is negative and relatively small). However, the positive DS_surr is much larger in magnitude than the negative DS_sys, so the total entropy change DS_total = DS_sys + DS_surr is positive. Because DS_total > 0, the reaction is spontaneous.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Recognises entropy is positive.

For Merit:
- Explains entropy for system and surroundings.

For Excellence:
- Fully justifies spontaneity.

questions.text:
The table gives electron configurations of three elements.

Krypton, Kr: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p6
Argon, Ar: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6
Sulfur, S: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4

When considering the 3p4 part of the electron configuration of sulfur, what is represented by:
3
p
4
questions.expectedAnswer: 3 = the third energy level/shell. p = the p subshell/orbital type. 4 = the number of electrons in this subshell.

questions.text: Arrange Kr, Ar, and S in order of decreasing first ionisation energy. Justify your order using periodic trends.
questions.expectedAnswer: Order of decreasing first ionisation energy: Ar > Kr > S. Ar has the highest IE because it is a noble gas with a full n=3 outer shell (very stable electron configuration) and a relatively small atomic radius. Kr also has a full outer shell but its outer (4p) electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded by additional inner shells, so less energy is required to remove an electron. S has the lowest IE of the three because it has only 6 electrons in its outer shell (3p4), which is a less stable configuration and the outer electron is more easily removed.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Recognises one factor.

For Merit:
- Explains with two factors.

For Excellence:
- Justifies for all three.

questions.text:
The two possible shapes of bromine trifluoride, BrF3, are T-shaped and trigonal planar. Both are based on trigonal bipyramidal electron arrangement.

Research shows BrF3 is polar.

Compare the two shapes to identify which would result in a polar molecule.

Refer to bond polarity and arrangement of bond dipoles.
questions.expectedAnswer: In a trigonal planar arrangement, the three Br-F bond dipoles are arranged symmetrically at 120 degrees to one another and cancel, giving no net dipole (non-polar). In the T-shaped arrangement (with two lone pairs occupying equatorial positions of the trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry), the three Br-F dipoles do not cancel — the axial Br-F dipoles oppose each other but the equatorial Br-F dipole is unopposed — giving a net dipole moment. Because BrF3 is observed to be polar, its molecular shape must be T-shaped, not trigonal planar.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Identifies polarity of each shape.

For Merit:
- Compares using dipole arrangement.

For Excellence:
- Full explanation with lone pair positions.

questions.text:
Identify all types of attractive forces between particles of these substances in their liquid state.

Ethylamine, CH3CH2NH2 (bp 17 degrees C)
Hydrogen bromide, HBr (bp -67 degrees C)
Pentane, C5H12 (bp 36 degrees C)
questions.expectedAnswer: Ethylamine, CH3CH2NH2: hydrogen bonding (via N-H), permanent dipole-dipole, London dispersion forces. Hydrogen bromide, HBr: permanent dipole-dipole and London dispersion forces (no hydrogen bonding — the H-Br bond is too weakly polar and Br is not N/O/F). Pentane, C5H12: London (dispersion) forces only.

questions.text: Explain the difference in the boiling points of ethylamine and hydrogen bromide.
questions.expectedAnswer: Ethylamine (bp 17 degrees C) has a much higher boiling point than hydrogen bromide (bp -67 degrees C). Ethylamine molecules can form hydrogen bonds between the N-H of one molecule and the lone pair on N of another molecule, which are strong intermolecular forces requiring significant energy to overcome. HBr only has weaker permanent dipole-dipole attractions and London dispersion forces; it cannot hydrogen-bond because Br is not electronegative enough (and is not N, O, or F). The stronger hydrogen bonds in ethylamine mean more energy is needed to separate the molecules, giving a higher boiling point.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Recognises H-bonding is stronger.

For Merit:
- Explains why ethylamine has higher bp.

questions.text: Explain why the boiling point of pentane is higher than that of hydrogen bromide.
questions.expectedAnswer: Pentane (C5H12, bp 36 degrees C) has only London dispersion forces, whereas HBr (bp -67 degrees C) has both dipole-dipole and London dispersion forces. Despite HBr having dipole-dipole attraction in addition to dispersion forces, pentane's much larger electron cloud (more electrons, larger surface area) produces significantly stronger total London dispersion forces than the combined intermolecular forces of the small HBr molecule. Because pentane's overall intermolecular forces are stronger, more energy is needed to separate the molecules and it has a higher boiling point.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Recognises size/electron cloud.

For Merit:
- Explains chain length gives stronger forces.

For Excellence:
- Compares all three.

questions.text:
The enthalpy of combustion of ethanol, C2H5OH, was determined experimentally. The ethanol was combusted to heat water.

Data: initial water temp = 20.5 degrees C, final = 28.7 degrees C, initial mass of burner and ethanol = 58.2 g, final = 57.6 g.

The student calculated DcH(C2H5OH(l)) = -726 kJ mol-1.
Specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 J g-1 degC-1.
M(C2H5OH) = 46.1 g mol-1

Calculate the mass of the water in the beaker.
questions.expectedAnswer: Mass of ethanol burned = 58.2 - 57.6 = 0.600 g. n(ethanol) = 0.600 / 46.1 = 0.01302 mol. Energy released = n x DcH = 0.01302 x 726 = 9.45 kJ = 9450 J. Temperature change DT = 28.7 - 20.5 = 8.2 degrees C. Using q = mcDT: 9450 = m x 4.18 x 8.2. m = 9450 / (4.18 x 8.2) = 9450 / 34.28 = 276 g of water.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- One step correct.

For Merit:
- Correct process with one error.

For Excellence:
- Correct mass.

questions.text:
Which quantity would have been a source of error in the calculated enthalpy value?

    temperature change of water          mass of fuel combusted

Explain your choice.
questions.expectedAnswer: Temperature change of water. Heat is lost to the surroundings (beaker, air) so the measured temperature change is less than the actual heat produced. This makes the calculated enthalpy less exothermic than the true value.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Identifies temperature change and ONE reason.

For Merit:
- Explains ONE reason for the error.
